The Royal Foundation. From the Tantra of the Three Roots: The nature of the unerring foundational system of medicine and astrology, its defining characteristics and valid reasoning, and the methods of study therein shall be explained from the ground up. First, regarding the nature of the foundational system:

Ka. From the intermediate chapter on medicine and astrology: The natural condition of the body, the causes and conditions of illness, the signs of illness, and the four types of treatment are explained. Regarding the natural condition of the body, the basis from which the body arises, and

Ga. From the immediate chapter on medicine: The five types of nectar substances, the distinctions among living things, the section on diet, the section on conduct, and the types of medicinal substances are explained. Within each of these, as explained one by one:

And, wishing to perceive the nature of things through reasoning, this text will be explained. For one who wishes to become skilled in the essential points of the oral instructions, it is first necessary to become acquainted with the root text to be explained.
Here, since it is difficult to explain without being acquainted with the text, the identity of the root text to be explained is called the Four Tantras. The meaning of the name: the definition of "tantra" is the inseparable connection of cause and result together.
From the Root Tantra: "Thus have I heard at one time. The Blessed One, renowned as the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel, skilled in the names of medicines for gods and humans, came to be known by that name. At the time when this Wish-Fulfilling Jewel, having entered into such an expanse, acted as the physician of all beings — at that time..."

[Human capacity:] Although the scriptures of established knowledge are present, it is difficult to find a reliable basis for examining them. From among the sutras of the Perfection of Wisdom, one should sometimes look to what the Tathagata's speech has firmly and unmistakably established as the direct subject matter; sometimes one should look to what has been taught in the manner of an explanatory tradition, where the basis was laid by the Able One and the meaning of the text is explained extensively; sometimes one should seek to expand upon it; and sometimes one should look to what has been taught in the manner of establishing philosophical tenets. If one does not know the established knowledge, one will fail to understand the meaning of the text. If one looks at the Perfection of Wisdom sutras without discernment, one should view all phenomena as empty, unattached to any philosophical position. When looking at the Perfection of Wisdom sutras from the side of philosophical tenets, one should look from the side of compassion. Looking at all phenomena as empty, unattached to any position — viewing it from that angle is the Perfection of Wisdom; and looking from the side of compassion — viewing it from that angle is the Perfection of Skillful Means.

[Remaining dwelling:] It is taught that one should apply the connections of the categories of the deceased nun's visionary tent. In looking at the categories: the Four Tantras — the Root Tantra, the Explanatory Tantra, the Oral Instruction Tantra, and the Subsequent Tantra — when looking at the Root Tantra, one should look at the texts in which the Indian and Tibetan scholars who arose from the Root Tantra explained the meaning of the Root Tantra extensively.

In order to clarify the characteristics that arise from analysis, and for the purpose of extensively explaining the meaning of the text as described, this work has been composed by drawing upon the teachings of kind masters and accomplished scholars.

In that regard, the first topic is a brief summary of the essential points of the Root Tantra; the second is an extensive explanation of the meaning of the Explanatory Tantra; the third is an explanation of the essential points of the Oral Instruction Tantra; and the fourth is an explanation of the meaning of the Subsequent Tantra.

As for the first: the outline of the Root Tantra is organized around three themes — the ground, which is birth; the path, which is healing; and the fruit, which is liberation. Under birth, the origins of the body are explained; under healing, tastes and potencies are explained; and under liberation, there are two aspects: ultimate liberation and provisional liberation.

As for the second, the Explanatory Tantra: it contains three main sections — an explanation of the nature of the body, an explanation of the causes and conditions of disease, and an explanation of the methods of medical treatment. Each of these is explained in detail.

Regarding the nature of the body: the manner of the body's composition, the impermanent body, the formations of the body, and the body of interdependent origination are explained.

Regarding the causes and conditions of disease: the distinction between primary causes and conditions, the classifications of disease, and the origins of disease are explained.

Regarding the methods of medical treatment: the maintenance of foundational health, the methods of treating illness, and the distinctions among foods and medicines are set forth.

This text is an excerpt from a learned commentary on the Four Medical Tantras, spoken by the Sugatas of boundless realms, which illuminates the names and meanings of medicinal substances — a work that gathers the essence of the nectar of excellence. Without the guide of a skilled teacher, one cannot understand the nature of medicine merely from names alone.

From that text, in order to clearly illuminate — not merely through surface names, but through the individual natures of each category of medicine and their respective functions — this lamp of excellent explanation was established on firm ground. Before the face of the omniscient teacher, the supreme Victor, the White Moon:

The compassionate Sugata, most cherished, has composed a commentary on the meaning of the vast teachings. This lamp that dispels the darkness of the mind, which enables true understanding, is well and auspiciously explained by its fine title.

A supremely learned scholar, endowed with knowledge and virtue, is skilled in the meanings of that text. The lord of accomplishment, supreme in qualities, has illuminated it with the light of supreme wisdom. This text, like a wish-fulfilling jewel, clearly reveals the names, meanings, and all the functions of the thirty-three categories of medicinal substances.

In the noble tradition as proclaimed by the Victorious One, the word was bestowed from the mouth of Shenrab. As it is clearly set forth in this text of excellent explanation — may it enter the mind and may understanding arise.

This is a question-and-answer commentary on the Root Tantra of the Four Medical Tantras composed by Yuthok, the All-Good one who is the essence of the Three Baskets of teachings. It is an explanatory note on the Eight-Limbed Ambrosia Essence tantra, which is the basis of the medical tantras.

Question: In brief, what is the nature of this tantra, which sets out the four foundations of medical knowledge — the way the body exists, the causes and conditions of illness, the signs of illness, and the methods of treatment?

Answer: In brief, this root text, which is the essence of all the writings of the Root Tantra, has six chapters. The first chapter explains the history and general meaning of the Root Tantra. The second, concerning how the body exists, explains the constitution of a human body along with how it abides. The third, concerning the causes and conditions of illness, explains the sequence of causes and conditions of illness in the bodies of beings who have erred in their way of living or have overstepped due time. The fourth, concerning the signs of illness, gives a concise explanation of those signs. The fifth, concerning the methods of treatment, explains the manner of treatment presented in this tantra. The sixth presents the final concluding words of confidence in the ultimate result.

Question: How is the first chapter of the Root Tantra explained?

Answer: The first chapter of the Root Tantra contains two things: an account of the origin of this text, and an explanation of the general meaning of the chapter in terms of words and meaning. Within the first of these, there are two parts: the manner in which this text was spoken by the Buddha, and the manner in which it came to living beings. Regarding the first — the manner in which it was spoken by the Buddha — the lord Yuthok taught and instructed gods and sages immediately upon his passing, saying to apply it to the science of the ambrosia of healing, and he explained how it would sustain life to its full extent.

Question: What is the explanation of the general meaning and words of the chapter?

Answer: Here, in the general meaning of the chapter, the commentary on the text is given in brief under three important divisions: first, explaining the divisions of the chapter's sections of the text; second, further explaining the essence of the text within this chapter; and third, summarizing the ultimate intended meaning at the end of the chapter.

The commentary on the root and foundational tantras; the exposition of medicine. All these teachings, gathered into a single root of medicine that cannot be perceived by ordinary means, [the master] departed to the realm of Mahādeva of primordial wisdom and invited there the emanation-bodies of the five buddha families. Thus: [mantra syllable] 12

The teaching on the combination of five syllables, which is comparable to the compound of clove, lapis lazuli, saffron, and the sour substances: In this way, since the five-fold combination is taught in the foundational tantra, one should abandon the two extremes.

The path for treating children's diseases is taught here in four stages: first, the growth of the body; second, the diminishment of the body; third, well-being; fourth, the basis of disease. Of these, the first — because it is impermanent — the growth of the body is to be purified through wisdom.

The exposition of the field of the science of healing: In this way, the science of healing abides in a field [of practice], and the principal transmissions came down through the old and new Yutok [Yönten Gönpo], and from the key points of the scriptures of the Victorious Ones, all the oral instructions of the hearing lineage have been gathered together.

The teaching that gathers the oral instructions into a single root of the foundational tantra: Applying it to the mental cultivation of the perfections, joined with fasting practice, one should take it up with the mind of enlightenment. All the instructions and oral teachings of the root and foundational tantras are collected here.

The manner of performing the ritual sequence of the temple of medicine and astrology: Departing to the formless realm and merely inviting [the presence] back, one should perform the reliquary rites. The teaching on the sequence of how to practice the method path: One invites the form of the perfection of wisdom. This commentary, derived from the explanatory tantra, arose from the text in which the root of the science of medicine is arranged in the four tantras.

Thus, through the reasoning explained, it is established that all phenomena lack inherent existence. Therefore, if one wishes to realize the meaning of the ultimate nature of things, one must be skillful in method, and come to understand that all phenomena arising in dependence on causes and conditions are empty of inherent existence. [13]

Furthermore, the details concerning the nature of the body and related topics should be consulted in the extensive treatises that explain them. If one thoroughly understands the nature of all the teachings of the medical science as described, not only will the root cause of disease be eliminated, but all the subsidiary conditions that sustain it will also be pacified.

Therefore, if one wishes to uphold the tradition of medical science, one must become learned in the meaning of these Four Tantras, and having entered into them, must firmly establish an unshakeable foundation.

I too have composed this great commentary on the Four Tantras, the foundational text of medical science, known as the "Jewel Mirror that Dispels the Unceasing Darkness of Disease and Malevolent Forces," so that it may benefit all beings.

[Colophon:] Thus, with compassionate motivation, this work has been completed for the benefit of all. May it be accomplished without obstruction.

[21.] Concerning the companion and the equal, and the gurgling and the gurgling-butter lotus-force, the four surges of the heartbeat, together with the four downward-flowing [winds], the self-comfort and the stirring-force and the outer, inner, and middle breath-channels: the oral teaching of the explanatory [tantra] blazes forth as vital force, and the upper and lower [aspects], the white and clear, are all encompassed therein.

Regarding the melody: one's own gurgling and the upper surge of the heartbeat, together with the four downward-flowing [winds], and the equal [wind's] outer breath-channel's blazing vital force, upper and lower, together with the four surges of the heartbeat, the oral teaching blazes forth as vital force, upper and lower, white and clear, all encompassed.

The commentary-gurgling melody's channel blazes as vital force, upper and lower, white and clear fully encompassed; regarding the red territory and the outer breath-channel's blazing vital force and the channel's blazing vital force; regarding the melody: the equal [wind's] gurgling, the commentary's oral-channel blazes as vital force, upper and lower, white and clear, fully encompassed.

In order to explain that the ground (basis) is without eyes: Although the ground itself, which has become the root, is explained as being without eyes, currently among the proponents of various philosophical schools there are those who assert it as having eyes. Therefore, a refutation of those who assert this is presented here. With respect to those texts that speak of "the eyes of the deity of empty form" and those tantric scriptures that serve as the basis for explaining the luminous awareness as an object of the eyes of the empty form body, those who assert that it is not eyeless — since they appear to be unlearned regarding the meaning of tantric scriptures other than their own — the view of those who assert this appears to have not understood the intent of the text.

Having thus explained that the ground is without eyes, and with respect to the accepted position regarding the defining characteristics of the ground: Looking at those texts which accept that the ground is without eyes, the method by which one intends to refute the views of other proponents of philosophical schools — if one explains it through the logical sign of the ground being without eyes — even though the luminous awareness that has become the ground is explained in two ways, as having eyes and as not having eyes, whether it actually exists or does not exist is something explained from within the state of union (zung 'jug), and should be understood as not to be distinguished as separate. The ground remains without moving from the state of birthlessness and emptiness, and through the power of dynamic energy, it displays itself as the great luminosity. Thus it is stated.

The ground is explained as being without eyes, and from the ground the path extends, so that from the perspective of the path, eyes are said to exist. Thus it is stated. In this way, with respect to the ground of the tantric scriptures in which the ground is without eyes, by explaining that from the perspective of the path eyes are said to exist — establishing with certainty an explanation unique and uncommon to both the ground and the path with respect to whether eyes exist or not — the views of others are thereby refuted.

Homage and introduction: During the time of dwelling in that place, Söka Tingpa, relying on the basis of the secret mantra and knowledge that has the nature of suchness, explained through the conduct of the six spheres of Chakrasamvara, without contradiction, for the sake of the wisdom of self and other — for their benefit. Chapter 8, folio 19.

Revealing the very nature that is the groundless ground:
Swirling in the vast expanse of great bliss,
The wisdom blazed forth by the fire of tummo,
Beyond conceptual elaboration,
The great seal of spontaneously present clear light,
Endowed with the element of the arising ground —

Through these three bases, realization of dharmas is attained.
As the ground of the secret body, reaching its limits entirely,
It adorns limitless beings equal to space
With the inexhaustible ornament of the three kayas.
Through whatever pacifies all afflictions,
Causing increase, bringing under control,
And through wrathful means accomplishing
All activities —

To the Medicine King Buddha,
I bow with reverence and shall explain.
Relying on the inner basis of knowledge
Of ground, path, and fruition,
Having realized the nature of phenomena,
The single ground pervading the entire body —
All activities accomplished through the single ground
Are brought to their limit, and the vajra body
Is excellently explained as being attained.

What is explained here: The words of the tantra of complete liberation — the heart of the explanatory tantra — shall be set forth without error. The method by which one realizes the meaning of union by relying on the knowledge of the body as ground; the method of being freed from the stains that serve as the cause of ignorance by abiding in the root ground of the body — these shall be explained. Explained thus: The single ground — that which is the root serving as the ground of the body — the tantra of the vajra body is explained. The reason for the body possessing form, abiding in the ground of the dharma-possessor, and depending on the nature of the ground of the path, the explanation of the key point of the union of wisdom and skillful means for the sake of being accomplished — relying on that very ground which is the body's basis, the heart-essence of the tantra by which the fruition vajra body is accomplished is fully and completely expounded.

[Page 20 of a Tibetan medical commentary. The text is a dense passage discussing the path of beings, the methods of the Sugata (Buddha), the nature of merit and giving, and the qualities of noble teachers and their disciples. A close rendering follows:]

Looking upon it carefully: together with the auspicious and the greatly powerful, one sees the depth of that mixture. The brave and venerable of old observed the manner of the venerable one endowed with speech. The body of the supreme lord among men in his youth — through the line of his miraculous emanation lineage — the lord endowed with speech and the basis.

In the sequence of blazing [merit], even to the finest dust at the margins, those who are thoroughly pure by nature come to know the path of those who go to bliss (the Sugata). Those who have become suitable vessels for those of great obstacles on the path to the Sugata — may the supremely high venerable one bestow great generosity upon beings.

The signs along the path of human lineages, of gradations of merit and so forth — at the time of the blazing of the syllables of the root of beings, with the sound of reverence — the method on the path of the master of giving, through the power of the lord of beings who is skilled in the dance of the body and senses — the master of the sacred learning (tsuglag) of the suitable vessels.

The knowledge that gathers without relying on the ground of beings, the key paths in accord with the path of the master of giving, the supremely purifying path of all — the crown of the path of the royal mind that is most fully accomplished — the single master of the vast generosity that does not separate suitable vessels.

The root path of even the finest dust that does not accord with the root — at the time of the sound of the dance, the obstacles of the Sugata, with reverence — may the path of beings' lineages of the ground become bliss. The crown of the pure ground of giving on all the paths of beings.

The path of the Sugata for suitable vessels who do not remain apart — the body of the path of the sacred learning (tsuglag) of beings — the path of the lord of beings in the dance, the obstacle of the Sugata — the ground of the master of giving by the pure beings.

May the crown of the ground of beings' paths become powerful for those suitable vessels. May they be well. The venerable one's path of beings — through the master of giving of the Sugata's ground and crown and paths — the ground of the Sugata of the sacred learning and path of beings.

[Page 99] This passage deals with the foundational substances, causes, and conditions related to the Three Roots of the medical tantras — namely the tree, trunk, and branches — and discusses their comprehensive enumeration and classifications. The author presents a single unified account: the text explains the combinations of medicinal substances and their compounding methods, along with the weights and measures involved in their preparation.

The text goes on to explain the nature of the constituent elements, the methods for settling unclear points regarding the digestion and transformation of nutrients, and the five qualities that produce comfort and clarity. It discusses how these elements move through the channels on the right and left sides of the body, and how they relate to purification and the arising of well-being.

The commentary then addresses the analytical framework used to examine these topics, explaining the causes and conditions underlying the movement of bodily constituents, and how the medicinal substances interact within the body to produce their effects. Various classifications of remedies, their modes of action, and their relationship to the five elements are outlined.

The passage continues with discussions of methods of compounding and administering treatments, the role of diet and lifestyle, and the conditions necessary for therapeutic success, drawing on the traditional explanatory framework of the Four Medical Tantras commentary tradition.

The analysis of the established teaching: Without that, it has not been explained by us. Again and again may there be ease. The Dharma taught by the Tathagata — I shall explain it well. To those fortunate beings who have gone to bliss — [page number] 22.

[The remainder of the text deals with technical descriptions from a Tibetan medical commentary, discussing physiological concepts including bodily fluids (chu, "water/fluid"), bodily cavities and structures, conditions involving falling or descending substances, causal relationships, and the qualities of being "without compassion" (mi snying rje) in a technical diagnostic sense — likely referring to conditions or symptoms that do not respond to treatment or that are inauspicious. References to "father and mother" (yab yum) may indicate inherited constitutional factors. The text appears to enumerate clinical signs and their prognostic significance in the tradition of the Gyushi (Four Medical Tantras) commentary.]

The essence of the Victor's teaching, blessed by the compassion of the Three Jewels, imbued with the blessings of the three bodies of the Blissful One — this is that very thing. Trusting and showing reverence toward Avalokiteshvara, the Protector, who acts to heal the hosts of illness and impurity afflicting the realms of the world, and placing one's confidence in this guide to the meaning of the Root Tantra of medical science, which arose from the kindness and words of the victorious Blissful Ones:

From the Secret Oral Instruction Tantra of the Essence of Ambrosia, the Eight-Branched [Medicine], the first tantra — the Root Tantra — is to be explained. The Root Tantra has seven chapters: the chapter on the basis, the chapter on the path, and the chapter on the result. Within the chapter on the basis there is one chapter: the Summary chapter, which is the first chapter. Second, within the chapter on the path there are two chapters: the chapter on the basis of the body, and the chapter on the analysis of the body. The main path chapter has three chapters: the chapter on clarifying what is to be known, the chapter on the medical system of the body, and the chapter on methods of treatment. The chapter on the result has one chapter: the concluding chapter, which is the seventh chapter. So it is taught.

Now, the first chapter of the Root Tantra — the Summary chapter — is to be explained. In the context of the text itself, it is stated: "Here begins the first chapter of the Secret Oral Instruction Tantra of the Essence of Ambrosia, the Eight-Branched [Medicine] — the chapter of the Summary, the physician's complete knowledge." The term "complete knowledge" makes clear that this is the word of the omniscient one who knows all medical systems. Trusting in this teaching and textual guide, which arose from the Victor's oral instructions, and with reverence, holding in mind the suffering of impermanence and the poison of illness, if one familiarizes oneself with this system of medical science, one will enter the path of harmlessness and well-being. Based on the system of the Kurustra tradition, one should take good care of the body and its substances.

Thus, having set forth the intention in nine categories and ten, explained through the six key points of subject matter in sequence, the nature of what is to be known at each juncture is summarized here in brief.

Venerated by the mind, always praised for accomplishment — entering into the profound essence of the teaching of the Sugata, the supreme: knowing the root of all illness among the three [categories of] outer, inner, and other, and discerning it clearly — do not transgress the highest vows of the one who has gone forth.

The view, however great in any regard: in this place of birth within the sufferings of samsara of the six [types of] beings in one's own stream — purify all misdeeds and obscurations, abide by the commitments, and the path of all sins and obscurations—

Honor what approaches there: offer the seven-limbed prayer, and up to the ultimate point of the key-point of the outermost limit — dispelling the darkness of ignorance, the light of primordial wisdom — it is said that the ultimate state of abiding is this.

Brought into contact through lineage: abiding in the realization of non-duality, with great weariness of samsara, look toward the final view — the mind that does not know, not knowing the object of knowledge — through the nature of the body, come to understand and attain realization.

What is to be explained here: as is said from the lamp's brilliance — explain it openly without concealing — descending from the abode — in the preparation of the path.

Now, summarizing everything in brief: the key point of the speech of the Victorious Ones, which is to be realized — connected to the system of Dharma through various enumerations — it is said that the path of reasoning is explained for whoever is suitable.

Due to the significant damage, fading, and compressed nature of this manuscript page, only partial and approximate translation is possible for the legible sections:

The third topic is the explanation of the qualities of medicine, which has three parts: the qualities of roots, branches, and fruits of medicine. The first of these has two parts: incompatible and compatible qualities in relation to food.

Regarding the first — the explanation of the qualities of medicinal roots: Medicinal roots have two qualities — those that are incompatible with food, and those that are compatible with it.

The incompatible quality: In the case of medicinal roots that are cooling in nature, if any cold food is combined with them, it will be harmful to the illness.

The second, the compatible quality: Likewise, if any warm food is combined with cooling medicinal roots, it will be beneficial for the illness.

The second section — the explanation of the qualities of medicinal branches: Medicinal branches also have two qualities — incompatible and compatible with food. The incompatible quality: if any loose or moving food is combined with branch medicines, it will be harmful to the illness. The compatible quality: if any astringent or sharp food is combined with branch medicines, it will be beneficial for the illness.

The third section — the explanation of the qualities of medicinal fruits: Medicinal fruits also have two qualities — incompatible and compatible with food. The incompatible quality: if any other food whatsoever is combined with fruit medicines, it will be harmful to the illness. The compatible quality: if any astringent or sharp food is combined with fruit medicines, it will be beneficial for the illness.

Regarding the vital point of the spleen: If the spleen is harmed, blood flows abundantly and intolerable suffering arises.

Regarding the vital point of the blood-bile-kidneys: If the vital point of the blood-bile is touched, bile-like conditions arise, and sourness and discomfort result. If the vital point of the kidneys is touched, the root channels are harmed.

Regarding the vital point of the omentum: If the vital point of the omentum is touched, discharge results.

Here is set forth an examination of the characteristics, diagnostic methods, and foundational matters pertaining to the sense organ of the tongue — this is explained in clear writing, and further elaborated as follows:

The characteristics of the tongue: One should recognize illness by observing whether the tongue is swollen, inflamed, moist, wet or dry, and by examining its color — whether white, yellow, red, blue, and so forth — and by looking at the front and back portions of the tongue.

Thus the method of examining the tongue: By observing the color of the tongue, one can recognize disease. A white tongue is a sign of phlegm disorders (beken). A yellow tongue is a sign of bile disorders (tripa) and related conditions. A red tongue is a sign of blood disorders and lung diseases and related conditions. A blue tongue is a sign of wind disorders (lung) and liver diseases and related conditions. A black tongue is a sign of a ruptured hollow organ and a sign of hopeless conditions. Whatever the condition of the tongue, one should look at whether the papillae of the tongue are prominent or reduced, and whether papillae are present or absent, and thereby recognize the disease.

Furthermore, by observing whether the tongue is moist or dry, one may recognize disease: A moist tongue indicates that vitality is present and moisture has arisen on the tongue. A dry tongue is a sign of reduced bodily fluids and of reversal between heat and cold and related conditions. A swollen tongue is a sign of phlegm disorders. A tongue that is pale and then inflamed is a sign of blood and bile disorders and related conditions.

In this way, the examination of the tongue to recognize disease is of great importance, and every physician must know it.

Third, the brief summary has two parts: the preliminary and the main body. The first, the brief exposition, has three sections: the nature of the body, the nature of disease, and the nature of healing. The first, the nature of the body, has two parts: definition and classification. As for the definition: the definition of the nature of the body is the very body of a sentient being endowed with the five foundations. The five foundations are: the three humors (wind, bile, and phlegm); the refined essence of food; blood; flesh; fat; bone; marrow; and the six reproductive constituents. As for the classification, the classification of the nature of the body has three divisions: 160
the basis-body, the causal-body, and the resultant-body. Because if one knows the basis-body, one can maintain freedom from illness; if one knows the causal-body, one can identify and eliminate the causes and conditions of disease; and if one knows the resultant-body, one can overcome all diseases and afflictions — therefore one must know these three. Of these three, the basis-body is said to be the most important. The basis-body also has two parts: the outer basis and the inner basis. Regarding the outer basis: it has two aspects, name and strength. The meaning of the name:
The basis-body is known as such at the time it is first constituted by the fundamental body. Strength is known as the sequential capacity of the body to perform its functions. The inner basis has two parts: location and description. As for location: the heart, liver, lungs, kidneys, and the foundational organs are the locations. As for description: with the navel as the base, the location of the two kidneys — their color, shape, and size — are described as identical to one another.
The nature of disease has two parts: definition and classification. As for the definition: the definition of the nature of disease is precisely the arising of a disturbance with causes and conditions that harm and injure the body. As for classification, there are three: diseases of the mind, diseases of speech, and diseases of the body. Regarding the nature of healing: it has two parts, definition and classification. As for the definition: the definition of healing is precisely that which, by eliminating the causes and conditions that harm and injure the body of the patient, serves as the means to generate well-being. [Page 1] If someone were to argue here: Is this not a traditional method that has been thoroughly established and tested by experienced physicians over many centuries, refined through practice and verified through direct experience? That would follow as a consequence. If it is a method verified through direct experience, it would then be established as true. That is not established, however — it is merely a tradition that has gained credibility and wide renown, passing from one neighboring physician to another like an echo from a cliff face, propagating outward, and so it does not become established as genuinely true. If someone argues: Since it is known to all and worthy of trust, is it not therefore true? If that were so, then it would absurdly follow that even erroneous traditions, since they are known to all and worthy of trust, would become true. That is not the case — it seems that two things are required: that something be widely known and worthy of trust, and that it be established without contradiction in its actual meaning. If someone argues: Is it not a tradition whose practice is grounded in truth and established through reasoning and verified through experience? That is unreasonable. The Root Tantra. The chapter of explicit statement: Chapter One. The Noble King of Medical Treatises, the Supreme Essence of Gold — the revealed meaning of the glorious Four Tantras — thus it is contained herein.

From the Four Tantras — comprising the Root Tantra, the Explanatory Tantra, the Oral Instruction Tantra, and the Subsequent Tantra — here is the first chapter of the Root Tantra, which sets forth the nature of the body as the foundation of medicine.

In the place where divine-natured persons gather, honored by those learned in the fields of knowledge, the compassionate divine physician Yuthok, who compiled the teachings of the Buddha — the great lord and king of medicine — from the Root Tantra, Chapter One: the chapter that teaches the nature of the body.

Within this first chapter of the Root Tantra, there are two parts: the explanation of the meaning of the words, and the explanation of the divisions. The first part has two sections: a brief explanation and an extensive explanation.

The brief explanation: If one does not understand the actual nature of medicine in what one currently perceives, one will engage in a battle devoid of truth. Therefore one must know well the actual nature of medicine.

Accordingly, regarding the nature of the body, there are two aspects. Under the two foundations — the foundation of how the body is formed, and the foundation of how disease arises — the first, the foundation of the body's formation, has two parts: the arrangement of the five elements and the three humors.

Regarding the five elements: there are five that give and five that receive. The five that give are earth, water, fire, wind, and space. The five that receive are: earth, which gives solidity to the body; water, which gives moisture to the body; fire, which gives warmth to the body; wind, which gives movement to the body; and space, which gives room to the body.

The arrangement of the three humors is: wind (rlung), bile (mkhris pa), and phlegm (bad kan).

Now, the detailed explanation of urine will be set forth under five headings: (1) the meaning of urine associated with delusion; (2) the meaning of differentiating urine by its conditions; (3) the meaning of the color, smell, and appearance of urine; (4) the meaning of pain associated with urination; (5) the meaning of urinary retention. Page 487.

These five are explained as follows. Regarding urine associated with delusion, the Ambrosia of Five Hundred states: "The urine called 'essence urine' upon contact is called urine associated with delusion." Although it says "held like ambrosia," what is meant by the phrase "the essence urine upon contact is called urine associated with delusion" is that the urine is so named because it is the essential urine of urine itself.

Regarding the differentiation of urine according to its dependent conditions, the Ambrosia of Five Hundred states that urine is differentiated from its conditions. Urine is classified from among the types of urine, and the conditional urine is further subdivided: there is the urine of the foundational basis, the urine of the intermediate stage, and the urine of the final stage—thus three divisions. Regarding color, smell, and appearance: the colors of urine are four—white, red, yellow, and blue; regarding smell, there are two—fragrant and foul; regarding appearance, there are three—swirling like muddy water, moist, and dry.

Regarding the meaning of pain in urination: there is pain like bubbles agitated as if by fire, and pain that flows down like a flat stream. Regarding the meaning of urinary retention: the causes of urinary retention are two—inability to pass urine and inconstancy in passing urine. Inability to pass urine also has two causes: conditions related to a vital point of the body, and conditions related to illness. In this way, the section on urine is concluded.

In this section the topic of urine has been explained. Following that, regarding the basis of urine: the basis of urine has two causes—the root cause of the basis of urine and the activating cause of the basis of urine.

Now, the classification of medicinal substances will be explained. This section sets forth the teaching on medicinal bases according to the manner of quintessential instructions that illuminate the meaning of the Four Tantras. In the section on signs, the classification of medicinal bases was summarized briefly. Therefore, regarding the classification of medicinal bases, there are two categories: general and specific. Speaking generally, all medicinal bases possess two kinds of distinguishing characteristics: those of their inherent nature and those of their potency. The distinguishing characteristics of inherent nature rest upon the natures that partake of earth, water, fire, wind, and space, and upon natures that have become antidotal; from these arise distinguishing characteristics of form such as taste, smell, shape, and texture, and colors including blue, yellow, red, white, green, and yellowish-white. The distinguishing characteristics of potency, resting upon taste, smell, form, and texture, include the natures of cold, heat, dryness, moisture, smoothness, roughness, sharpness, dullness, neutrality, ease of use, heaviness, and lightness.

Speaking specifically, medicinal bases are classified into the categories of roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, heartwood, bark, and so forth, and within each of these there are further specific descriptions.

Regarding the category of roots: there are three kinds — root proper, trunk, and branches. Among roots, there are the underground-spreading roots and the above-ground roots. Among trunks, there are those that shed bark on the left and right and those that do not. Among branches, there are various distinguishing characteristics. The potencies and pharmaceutical classifications of all of these have already been explained clearly.

In the present context, the reasons for achieving deep understanding are to be explained as follows: When considering the methods for treating the sick in present circumstances, one must gain comprehension of the meaning of the Four Medical Tantras. As the Explanatory Tantra teaches: one must gain understanding of the methods by which diseases are resolved. As the Oral Instruction Tantra states: through knowledge of the pulse, one should understand the nature of the body. Therefore, a physician should become thoroughly familiar with the textual content of the Four Tantras, and with wisdom examine the condition of the patient, leading them onto the path of the healing science. Specifically, having gained understanding of the natural state of the three bodily humors — wind, bile, and phlegm — one must relate this to the causes and conditions underlying the origin of the disease and apply appropriate treatment. Through the methods of pulse examination, urine examination, and examination of the complexion, one should determine the precise nature of the disease and apply a method that is suitable.
Mere comprehension of the textual meaning of the Four Tantras is not sufficient; practical experience is of the utmost importance. Therefore, a physician endowed with good reasoning should train in the textual tradition of the Four Tantras and put them into practice. As the great masters of medicine have taught: if one is to engage in the work of benefiting others, one must first purify one's own mind, and then, abiding on the path that unites method and wisdom, engage in activities that bring benefit to others.

Here, in the explanation of the nature of the body: first, an explanation of the root of the body; second, an explanation of the basis of the body; third, an explanation of the elements of the body; fourth, an explanation of the causes of the body; fifth, an explanation of the conditions of the body; sixth, an explanation of the cooperative conditions of the body.

Regarding the explanation of the root of the body, there are two parts — the basis and the root. Regarding the explanation of the basis of the body, there are two parts: the primary basis and the subsidiary basis. The subsidiary basis is the basis of wind — it is the basis of wind or the elements residing in the bodily channels.

Regarding the explanation of the elements of the body: what arises from the body's basis is the food of the body, or that which follows after food. What arises from the root of the body is food, vital essence, and life-force together.

Regarding the explanation of the causes of the body: the primary cause is the basis of mind — it is the foundation of the mind residing in the bodily channels. The subsidiary cause is the basis of the body — it is the foundation of the body residing in the bodily channels.
